steps.title: Hello
steps.how_to: How to say hello at the right time of day, to one person or a whole room.
steps.intro: You'll learn which hello fits the hour, and how to greet everyone in a room at once. You'll say it every time you walk into a shop, a café or a taquería.
steps.notice: Buenos días goes until about noon, buenas tardes from noon until dark, and buenas noches once it's dark. Add a todos to greet the whole room, and a short buenas works at any hour.
steps.context: A quick buenas is enough when you walk into a small shop.

ask.said: Ves a una señora en la mañana. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You see a lady in the morning. What do you say?

ask.said: Entras a la sala de espera del doctor a la una. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You walk into the doctor's waiting room at one o'clock. What do you say?

ask.said: De noche ves a tu vecino. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: At night you see your neighbor. What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet everyone in the shop as you walk in.

steps.title: How are you
steps.how_to: How to say how you are when someone asks.
steps.intro: You'll be able to answer when someone asks how you are. People ask it in shops, at cafés and on the stairs.

examples.en: I'm fine, thanks, just working away.

steps.notice: To say how you are, start with estoy: estoy bien, estoy un poco cansada. A man says cansado and a woman says cansada.

ask.said: ¿Cómo estás hoy?
ask.en: How are you today?

ask.said: Hoy es un día difícil. ¿Cómo estás?
ask.en: Today's a hard day. How are you?

ask.said: Caminas todo el día. ¿Cómo estás?
ask.en: You've been walking all day. How are you?

mission.goal: Answer when someone asks how you are.

steps.title: Be polite
steps.how_to: How to choose between polite usted and friendly tú.
steps.intro: You'll learn two ways to ask how someone is, one polite and one friendly. You'll use the polite one with most adults you meet at the shop or the market.

examples.en: Good morning, ma'am. How are you?

steps.notice: With shopkeepers, older people and strangers, you say ¿cómo está? and ¿y usted? With friends, children and people your age who use tú with you first, it's ¿cómo estás? and ¿y tú?
steps.context: In Mexico, using usted is a sign of respect, not distance.

ask.said: Ves a un señor mayor en la plaza. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You see an older man in the plaza. What do you ask?

answer.en: Good afternoon, sir. How are you?

ask.said: Ves a tu amiga Ana. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You see your friend Ana. What do you ask?

ask.said: Un niño de tu calle dice hola. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: A kid from your street says hi. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Greet the shopkeeper politely and ask how they are.

say.en: Good morning, ma'am. How are you?

steps.title: Titles
steps.how_to: How to address people with joven, señor, señora, don and doña.
steps.intro: You'll be able to speak to people the way Mexicans do, with a title instead of a name. You'll use it with strangers, shopkeepers and older neighbors.
steps.notice: Use joven, señor or señora for people you don't know. Use don or doña with the first name for older people you know, like doña Lupita.
steps.context: Market vendors often call you joven, señorita, güero or güera, and it's friendly sales talk.

ask.said: Necesitas ayuda de un chico en la calle. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You need help from a young guy on the street. What do you say?

answer.en: Excuse me, could you help me?

ask.said: En la farmacia hay un señor. Es la tarde. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: There's a man at the pharmacy. It's the afternoon. What do you say?

ask.said: Ves a tu vecina mayor, Carmen, por la mañana. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You see your older neighbor, Carmen, in the morning. What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet the shopkeeper with a polite title.

steps.title: Goodbye
steps.how_to: How to say goodbye with que le vaya bien, and answer it.
steps.intro: You'll be able to leave a shop or say goodbye to a neighbor the way people do here. You'll also know how to answer when someone says it to you.

examples.said: Hasta luego. Que le vaya bien.

steps.notice: Learn que le vaya bien as one phrase, and change only le: te for a friend, les for a group. When someone says it to you, answer gracias, igualmente.
steps.context: People say goodbye when they leave a small shop.

ask.said: Sales de la taquería. ¿Qué dices al taquero?
ask.en: You're leaving the taquería. What do you say to the taquero?

answer.said: Buenas noches, que le vaya bien.
answer.en: Good night, have a good one.

ask.said: Tu amigo se va a casa. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: Your friend is heading home. What do you say?

answer.said: Nos vemos, que te vaya bien.

ask.said: Dos amigas se van. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: Two friends are leaving. What do you say?

answer.said: Hasta mañana, que les vaya bien.

mission.goal: Say goodbye to the shopkeeper as you leave.

say.said: Hasta luego. Que le vaya bien.

steps.title: Name
steps.how_to: How to say your name and ask for theirs.
steps.intro: You'll be able to give your name and ask the other person for theirs. You'll use it the moment you meet a neighbor or anyone new.

examples.en: My name's Rosa. Nice to meet you.

steps.notice: You give your name with me llamo, and ask it back with ¿y usted? or ¿y tú? To ask first, say ¿cómo se llama? with usted and ¿cómo te llamas? with a friend.

ask.said: ¿Cómo te llamas?
ask.en: What's your name?

ask.said: Conoces a un señor mayor. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You meet an older man. What do you ask?

ask.said: Conoces a un chico en una fiesta. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You meet a guy at a party. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor your name and ask theirs.

steps.title: Who are you
steps.how_to: How to say where you're from and where you live now, and ask the same back.
steps.intro: You'll be able to tell people where you're from and where you live now, then ask them. People ask this early on, so it's worth having ready.

examples.said: Soy de Toronto, pero ahora vivo aquí.
examples.en: I'm from Toronto, but I live here now.
I live right here, near the market.

steps.notice: Soy de and a place says where you're from, and vivo en or vivo aquí says where you live now. To ask back, add ¿y usted? or ¿y tú?
steps.context: Every address includes the colonia, which matters more than the street for finding a place.

ask.said: ¿Eres de aquí?
ask.en: Are you from here?

ask.said: ¿Dónde vives?
ask.en: Where do you live?

answer.en: I live in the … neighborhood. And you?

ask.said: Hablas con una señora en el mercado. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You're talking with a lady at the market. What do you ask?

answer.en: And where do you live, ma'am?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor where you're from and ask where they live.

say.said: Soy de …, pero ahora vivo aquí. ¿Y usted?
say.en: I'm from …, but I live here now. And you?

steps.title: Time here
steps.how_to: How to say how long you've been here, and ask someone else.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say how long you've been here and ask others the same. Neighbors and new friends ask this early on.

examples.en: How long have you been here?
How long have you been in Mexico?

examples.said: Llevo un mes en México. ¿Y tú?
examples.en: I've been in Mexico a month. And you?

steps.notice: Say llevo or tengo, then the time, then aquí or en México. To ask, start with ¿cuánto tiempo?: lleva with usted, llevas with a friend.
steps.context: People here often ask early on how long you've been here.

ask.said: ¿Eres nuevo en el barrio?
ask.en: Are you new in the neighborhood?

ask.said: ¿Llevas mucho tiempo en Oaxaca?
ask.en: Have you been in Oaxaca long?

answer.en: No, I've been in Oaxaca … months.

ask.said: Una chica en la plaza también es nueva. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: A girl in the plaza is new here too. What do you ask?

answer.en: And how long have you been here?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbor how long you've been here.

steps.title: Slower, please
steps.how_to: How to say you didn't understand and ask to hear it again, more slowly.
steps.intro: You'll learn the phrases to use the moment someone speaks too fast. You can say them at a taco stand, a counter or anywhere else.

examples.en: Could you say that again, please?
Could you say it again more slowly?

steps.notice: No entendí says you missed it, and ¿me lo puede repetir? asks to hear it again; add más despacio for slower. With a friend, it's ¿me lo puedes repetir?
steps.context: Newcomers are expected to ask, and most people slow down and rephrase gladly.

ask.said: La cajera habla muy rápido. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: The cashier is talking really fast. What do you say?

answer.en: I didn't get that. Could you say it again?

ask.said: Tu vecino dice algo y no entiendes. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: Your neighbor says something and you don't understand. What do you say?

answer.en: Sorry, can you say that again?

ask.said: El chofer repite, pero muy rápido. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: The driver says it again, but really fast. What do you say?

answer.said: Otra vez, más despacio, por favor.

mission.goal: Tell the taquero you didn't understand and ask for slower.

say.said: Perdón, no entendí. Más despacio, por favor.
say.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. More slowly, please.

steps.title: Pardon?
steps.how_to: How to use ¿mande? to ask for a repeat and to answer when someone calls you.
steps.intro: You'll learn one polite word that does two jobs. You can say it when you missed something, or when someone calls to you.

examples.en: Sorry? How many do you want?
Sorry? Could you tell me your name again?

steps.notice: ¿Mande? asks someone to say it again, and it's also how you answer when someone calls you. It's the polite choice with anyone, older people too.
steps.context: Asking ¿mande? is normal for a newcomer, and people take it well.

ask.said: El taquero dice algo muy rápido. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: The taquero says something really fast. What do you say?

ask.said: Doña Rosa dice tu nombre desde la puerta. ¿Qué contestas?
ask.en: Doña Rosa calls your name from the door. What do you answer?

ask.said: Una señora en el mercado habla y no entiendes. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: A woman at the market is talking and you don't understand. What do you say?

mission.goal: Ask a vendor to repeat what they said.

steps.title: Ask politely
steps.how_to: How to ask someone politely to do something with ¿me puede…?
steps.intro: You'll learn a simple pattern for polite requests. You can use it to ask for help, for a slower pace, or for almost anything.
steps.notice: Use puede with usted and puedes with a friend. The next verb always ends in -r, like ayudar, dar and hablar.

ask.said: No entiendes una dirección. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You can't make out an address. What do you ask?

answer.en: Could you write down the address, please?

ask.said: Quieres el número de tu vecino. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You want your neighbor's number. What do you ask?

ask.said: Tienes muchas bolsas y no puedes abrir la puerta. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You've got lots of bags and can't open the door. What do you ask?

answer.said: ¿Me puede abrir la puerta, por favor?
answer.en: Could you open the door for me, please?

mission.goal: Ask the ticket clerk to help you.

steps.title: Spell it
steps.how_to: How to spell words out loud with Spanish letter names.
steps.intro: You'll learn how to spell your name and ask how a word is spelled. You'll use it for forms, orders and new words.

examples.en: Could you spell your last name, please?

examples.said: Doble u, e, be grande, be grande.

examples.en: How do you spell it? With a B?

examples.said: Sí: be grande, a, ene, cu, u, e, te, a.
examples.en: Yes: B, A, N, Q, U, E, T, A.

steps.notice: Spanish letters have their own names, and the vowels sound like eh and ee. Say doble u for W, be grande for B and ve chica for V.
steps.context: B and V sound the same, so Mexicans say be grande and ve chica to tell them apart.

ask.said: Cuando deletreas, ¿cómo dices la V?
ask.en: When you spell, how do you say V?

ask.said: ¿Cómo deletreas «Bob»?
ask.en: How do you spell 'Bob'?

ask.said: Oyes la palabra «vaso». ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You hear the word 'vaso'. What do you ask?

answer.said: ¿«Vaso» se escribe con be grande o con ve chica?
answer.en: Is 'vaso' spelled with a B or a V?

mission.goal: Ask a neighbor how a word is spelled.

say.said: ¿Cómo se escribe? ¿Con be grande o con ve chica?
say.en: How do you spell it? With a B or a V?

steps.title: Excuse me
steps.how_to: How to pick the right excuse me: to get past, to get attention or after a bump.
steps.intro: English has one excuse me where Spanish has three. You'll be able to get through a crowded bus, call someone over, or say sorry after a bump.

examples.en: Excuse me, could you help me with something?

steps.notice: Con permiso is for getting past or leaving, disculpe gets someone's attention, and perdón is for after a bump. With a friend it's disculpa, and to a group, disculpen.
steps.context: People say con permiso whenever they pass someone or leave a table.

ask.said: Una señora está en la puerta. ¿Qué dices para pasar?
ask.en: A lady is standing in the doorway. What do you say to get by?

ask.said: Chocas con un señor en el mercado. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You bump into a man at the market. What do you say?

ask.said: Necesitas ayuda de dos chicas en la plaza. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You need help from two girls in the plaza. What do you say?

answer.en: Excuse me, could you help me?

mission.goal: Ask to get past people.

steps.title: Say it softly
steps.how_to: How to soften a request with momentito, poquito and ahorita.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask for a moment or say a little bit in a friendly, polite way. You'll hear it and use it at every counter and stand.

examples.said: Un poquito de salsa, por favor.

steps.notice: Adding -ito makes a request or an amount sound smaller and politer. It isn't literal: un momentito can be several minutes, and ahorita can mean now, soon or later.

ask.said: Buscas tu dinero en la tienda. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You're looking for your money in the store. What do you say?

ask.said: ¿Hablas español?
ask.en: Do you speak Spanish?

ask.said: ¿Cuándo vas a la tienda?
ask.en: When are you going to the store?

mission.goal: Ask the pharmacist to wait a moment.

steps.title: Order politely
steps.how_to: How to ask for food and drinks politely with me da.
steps.intro: You'll learn the phrase you'll use at every counter, taco stand and café. It lets you ask for what you want politely.

examples.said: Me da un pan dulce, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have a pan dulce, please?

examples.said: Me da una torta, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have a torta, please?

examples.said: Me da un agua, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have a water, please?

examples.said: Me da un boleto para Puebla, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have a ticket to Puebla, please?

steps.notice: Every order starts with me da, then what you want, and por favor. It's the polite way to ask a stranger for something across a counter.
steps.context: Orders usually start with a greeting, like buenas tardes.

ask.said: Tienes hambre en la taquería. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You're hungry at the taquería. What do you order?

answer.said: Me da tres tacos, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have three tacos, please?

ask.said: Estás en el café por la mañana. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You're at the café in the morning. What do you order?

answer.said: Me da un café, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have a coffee, please?

ask.said: Necesitas aspirinas en la farmacia. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You need aspirin at the pharmacy. What do you ask for?

answer.said: Me da unas aspirinas, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have some aspirin, please?

mission.goal: Order tacos at the stand.

say.said: Buenas tardes. Me da tres tacos, por favor.
say.en: Good afternoon. Can I have three tacos, please?

steps.title: How many
steps.how_to: How to order one of something or more than one.
steps.intro: You'll learn to order one thing or several. You'll say it every time you ask for tacos, a torta or a drink.

examples.said: Me da dos tacos, por favor.
examples.en: Can I have two tacos, please?
One coffee and two waters, right?

examples.said: Me da una torta y un agua.
examples.en: Can I have a torta and a water?

steps.notice: Use un for one masculine thing and una for a feminine one, like una torta; agua takes un. For more than one, add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant: tacos, limones.
steps.context: Limón in Mexico is the small green lime.

ask.said: Tú y dos amigos quieren tortas. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You and two friends want tortas. What do you order?

answer.said: Me da tres tortas, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have three tortas, please?

ask.said: Pides un café para ti y uno para Ana. ¿Qué dices?
ask.en: You're ordering a coffee for you and one for Ana. What do you say?

answer.said: Me da dos cafés, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have two coffees, please?

ask.said: Quieres mangos en el mercado. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You want mangoes at the market. What do you ask for?

answer.said: Me da tres mangos, por favor.
answer.en: Can I have three mangoes, please?

mission.goal: Order a torta and a water.

say.said: Me da una torta y un agua, por favor.
say.en: Can I have a torta and a water, please?

steps.title: Name the filling
steps.how_to: How to say what a taco, torta or drink is filled with or made of.
steps.intro: You'll learn to name the filling or flavor of what you order. You'll use it at the taco stand, the torta stand and the agua fresca counter.

examples.said: Tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
Un agua de jamaica, por favor.

steps.notice: The food comes first, then de, then the filling or flavor: tacos de pastor, torta de milanesa, agua de jamaica. It's the other way around from English.
steps.context: People also say tacos al pastor.

ask.said: ¿Qué tacos quieres?
ask.en: What kind of tacos do you want?

answer.said: Dos tacos de bistec, por favor.

ask.said: ¿Qué torta pides?
ask.en: What kind of torta are you getting?

answer.said: Una torta de jamón, por favor.

ask.said: ¿Qué agua fresca pides?
ask.en: What agua fresca are you getting?

answer.said: Un agua de horchata, por favor.

mission.goal: Order tacos with a filling you choose.

say.said: Me da dos tacos de bistec, por favor.
say.en: Can I have two steak tacos, please?

steps.title: With or without
steps.how_to: How to say with or without something when you order.
steps.intro: You'll get two small words that let you say how you want your food or drink. You'll use them when the taquero or the waiter asks what goes in it.
steps.notice: Con means with and sin means without. Both go straight before the food: con todo, sin cebolla, sin azúcar.
steps.context: Con todo means with onion and cilantro.

ask.said: ¿Quieres salsa en tu torta?
ask.en: Do you want salsa on your torta?

ask.said: ¿Quieres cilantro en tus tacos?
ask.en: Do you want cilantro on your tacos?

ask.said: ¿Cómo tomas el café?
ask.en: How do you take your coffee?

mission.goal: Order tacos and say what you don't want on them.

steps.title: A little extra
steps.how_to: How to ask for small things like a napkin with ¿me regala…?
steps.intro: You'll learn a soft way to ask for little extras at a stand or counter. It helps when you need a napkin, a bag or some water.

examples.en: Can I get your name, please?

steps.notice: Say ¿me regala…? and then the small thing you need. It doesn't mean it's free: you still pay for what has a price, and ¿me da…? works everywhere too.
steps.context: People use ¿me regala…? for small things, paid for or free.

ask.said: Quieres más salsa en la taquería. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You want more salsa at the taquería. What do you ask for?

answer.en: Could I get some more salsa?

ask.said: No tienes cuchara para la sopa. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You don't have a spoon for your soup. What do you ask for?

ask.said: Quieres un limón en la fonda. ¿Qué pides?
ask.en: You want a lime at the fonda. What do you ask for?

answer.en: Could I get a lime, please?

mission.goal: Ask the taquero for a napkin.

steps.title: When they ask
steps.how_to: How to answer when shop staff ask ¿qué buscaba?
steps.intro: You'll be able to answer when shop staff call you in and ask what you need. You'll hear it at shops and market stalls.

examples.en: Come on in! What are you looking for?

steps.notice: Shop staff ask in the past to sound softer. You answer in the present: say what you want, or that you're just looking.
steps.context: Shop and market staff call out ¡pásele! to bring you in.

ask.said: Buenas tardes, ¿qué buscaba?
ask.en: Good afternoon, what are you looking for?

ask.said: ¿Qué buscaba, joven?
ask.en: What are you looking for?

answer.said: Solo estoy viendo la fruta, gracias.
answer.en: Just looking at the fruit, thanks.

ask.said: Buenos días, ¿qué necesitaba hoy?
ask.en: Good morning, what do you need today?

mission.goal: Tell the shopkeeper you're just looking.

steps.title: How much
steps.how_to: How to ask the price of one thing or of several, and understand the answer.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what something costs, whether it's one thing or several. You'll use it at market stalls, shops and taco stands.
steps.notice: Ask ¿cuánto cuesta? for one thing and ¿cuánto cuestan? for several, with the thing after it. The answer starts the same way: cuesta treinta pesos, cuestan veinte.

ask.said: Quieres un café de olla. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You want a café de olla. What do you ask?

answer.en: How much is the café de olla?

ask.said: En el mercado ves unos mangos. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You see some mangoes at the market. What do you ask?

ask.said: Te gusta un sombrero en el mercado. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You like a hat at the market. What do you ask?

mission.goal: Ask the vendor how much something costs.

steps.title: Hear a price
steps.how_to: How to understand a price said aloud in pesos.
steps.intro: You'll be able to catch a total when someone says it, and say one back. You'll hear prices at every counter, stall and taco stand.

examples.en: That's a hundred and twenty pesos.

steps.notice: A total is son, the number, then pesos. From thirty-one on, the tens and units join with y, as in ochenta y cinco; from a hundred and one it's ciento, as in ciento veinte.
steps.context: The $ sign on a price here means pesos.

ask.said: Tres tacos de veinte pesos. ¿Cuánto es?
ask.en: Three tacos at twenty pesos each. How much is that?

ask.said: Dos tortas de cincuenta pesos. ¿Cuánto es?
ask.en: Two tortas at fifty pesos each. How much is that?

ask.said: Un pan de quince y un café de cuarenta. ¿Cuánto es?
ask.en: A fifteen-peso pastry and a forty-peso coffee. How much is that?

mission.goal: Ask what you owe and catch the total.

steps.title: Card or cash
steps.how_to: How to ask if you can pay by card, and understand card or cash.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask whether a place takes cards, and answer when they ask how you're paying. You'll use it at stalls, shops and cafés.

examples.en: Excuse me, do you take cards?

steps.notice: Ask ¿aceptan tarjeta? before you pay. You'll hear con tarjeta for card and en efectivo for cash, and nada más efectivo means cash only.
steps.context: Cash is still everyday money at markets and stalls.

ask.said: Solo tienes tu tarjeta en la taquería. ¿Qué preguntas?
ask.en: You only have your card at the taquería. What do you ask?

answer.en: Excuse me, do you take cards here?

ask.said: ¿Cómo pagas el café hoy?
ask.en: How are you paying for the coffee today?

ask.said: ¿Cómo pagas en el mercado?
ask.en: How do you pay at the market?

mission.goal: Ask the shopkeeper if they take cards.

say.en: Excuse me, do you take cards?
